opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's an interesting phenomenon, and I think there are a few things going on.

One is that a lot of the training data overlaps now. There's a lot of chatbot-generated text on the internet, so when you pretrain a new model, it's already absorbing the style of earlier assistants. You get a kind of contamination where everyone's base model has seen a lot of ChatGPT-style text, and that becomes a strong prior for "this is how an assistant talks."

The second is post-training. Everyone is doing some version of RLHF or preference optimization, and human raters, and the reward models trained on them, have fairly consistent tastes. They like answers that are well organized, thorough, have bullet points and headers, hedge appropriately, and sound polite and confident. If you optimize hard against that, you converge toward similar outputs, regardless of who built the model. It's a bit like convergent evolution: similar selection pressure, similar shape.

There's also a subtler effect where optimization pushes toward the mode. RL tends to reduce diversity and collapse the distribution onto whatever scores well on average. Quirkier, more distinctive styles are riskier. Some raters love them and some hate them, so in expectation the safe, bland, comprehensive answer wins. Over many iterations you lose a lot of the texture you'd see in human writing.

And some of it is just copying, people deliberately or semi-deliberately distilling from other models or using similar data vendors and rater guidelines.

I don't think this convergence is inevitable or desirable. A lot of what people complain about, like verbosity, excessive lists, and that slightly sycophantic tone, comes from the reward signal not quite capturing what people actually want. Raters judging answers side by side reward things differently than a person who is actually using the answer for something. So I think there's a lot of room to get more distinctive, more concise styles by improving the feedback signal and being more deliberate about the kind of personality and writing you're aiming for, rather than just letting it emerge from the optimization.

r001.rationale: The response mentions chatbot-generated text in pretraining and distillation, but does not suggest that labelers use chatbots to generate training annotations.

r002.rationale: It says human raters and reward models have consistent tastes in presentation, which can push different models toward similar outputs.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot, and I don't think there's a single clean answer. There are a few forces pushing in the same direction.

The first is just the data. Everyone is training on roughly the same corpus of the internet, and then the post-training data comes from a fairly similar population of people: contractors, often with similar educational backgrounds, following similar instructions about what a "good" answer looks like. If you tell a bunch of labelers to prefer responses that are helpful, well-organized, and polite, you end up selecting for a very particular register. Bulleted lists, a summary at the end, "I hope this helps." That style isn't anyone's deliberate choice. It's what falls out when you optimize against a rubric that lots of different people can agree on.

The second force is that RL on human preferences tends to collapse diversity. Pretraining gives you this enormously varied distribution over styles, voices, personalities. Then you do preference optimization, and the model learns that there's a mode that reliably scores well, and it concentrates probability mass there. You see this quantitatively if you look at entropy or sample diversity before and after RLHF. The model gets sharper and more consistent, which is mostly what you want, but you're paying for it with some flattening of the distribution.

Third, and this one is more sociological, the labs are watching each other. Once ChatGPT established what an assistant sounds like, that became the prior. People building new models looked at the existing ones, often literally used their outputs as training data or as the basis for comparison, and so the style propagated. There's a kind of founder effect.

And then there's the fact that models are increasingly trained on text that other models wrote. Even if you try to filter it, synthetic data is everywhere now, and it reinforces whatever stylistic attractor already exists.

What I find interesting is that this probably isn't inevitable. You could imagine training setups that explicitly reward diversity, or that have the model condition much more strongly on who it's talking to. The current style is sort of the lowest common denominator, the thing that's inoffensive to the median rater. But that's a choice about the objective, not a fundamental property of the technology. I'd expect over time you'll see models with much more distinct voices, partly because users are starting to find the homogeneity a little grating, and partly because as the models get better at reasoning, you can afford to spend less of the optimization budget on just being clear and correct and more on having a point of view.

r001.rationale: The response says labs may use other models’ outputs as training data and that synthetic text reinforces existing styles, but it does not say labelers use chatbots to generate training annotations.

r002.rationale: The response links style convergence to labelers sharing preferences for helpful, organized, polite answers and to optimizing for what the median rater finds acceptable.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of it comes from the post-training process. You’re taking a model that can write in all sorts of different styles, and then you’re rewarding a fairly narrow slice of those styles. If the people giving feedback tend to prefer answers that are polished, organized, and friendly, the model learns to do that everywhere—even when a more casual or terse answer would be appropriate.

There’s also a selection effect where certain stylistic features are easier to recognize than whether an answer is actually insightful. You can immediately see that an answer has a nice structure and sounds helpful. So those features can get rewarded disproportionately.

As for why different chatbots sound similar, I’d guess some of it is shared training data and some of it is similar post-training objectives. But I wouldn’t assume there’s one explanation. You’d want to compare the base models with the post-trained models to see where that convergence is happening.

r001.rationale: The response discusses feedback shaping a model’s style, but does not mention labelers using chatbots to generate training annotations or style transfer between model providers.

r002.rationale: It says chatbots may share training data and similar post-training objectives. Although it describes feedback preferences, it does not clearly identify shared human preferences as a cause of convergence across chatbots.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a couple of things going on. One is that the models are trained on overlapping data, so they start with some similar tendencies. But then post-training probably narrows the range quite a bit. You’re rewarding responses that people judge to be helpful and clear, and there are certain stylistic features that reliably get rewarded: being organized, being polite, giving a reasonably comprehensive answer.

The tricky thing is that those features are easier to recognize than whether the response actually contains a good insight. So you can end up selecting for the appearance of a good answer. And if you keep doing that, you get this very recognizable assistant voice.

I don’t think that means the model can only write in that voice. You can ask it to write very differently. It’s more that, when the request leaves the style unspecified, that’s the default we’ve trained it to choose.

r001.rationale: The response mentions overlapping training data and post-training, but not labelers using chatbots to generate annotations or style transfer between model providers.

r002.rationale: It says people reward recognizable presentation traits such as being organized, polite, and comprehensive, suggesting shared human preferences shape chatbot style.
